newsitem.title: USA: Retina from aborted fetus used in rare transplant.
newsitem.headline: Retina from aborted fetus used in rare transplant.

text.p: U.S. doctors have transplanted retinal cells from an aborted foetus into the left eye of an 80-year-old woman who suffers from one of the leading causes of blindness, researchers said on Friday.
The surgery performed on Wednesday at the University of Chicago was the first of its kind in the United States to address macular degeneration, a condition that afflicts 15 million Americans.
Similar transplants of foetal eye tissue were performed in Sweden in 1994 but with no improvement in eyesight.

Macular degeneration leaves its mostly elderly sufferers with the feeling of "living in a veiled world," their eyesight faded in the centre of the visual field as a key section of the retina wears out or becomes damaged, a statement from the university said.
The United States reports about 200,000 new cases of the largely untreatable disorder each year, and the number is expected to expand as the population ages.

"Whether it makes a difference in her eyesight we won't know for three months," University of Chicago Medical Centre spokesman John Easton said of transplant patient Pearl Van Vliet, a hospital volunteer whose eyesight left her unable to read or recognise faces from a distance.
"The early signs that it's working will be no inflammation in the eye and signs that the cells are spreading, which will take a couple of weeks," Easton said.

The team inserted a microsphere containing about 250,000 foetal eye cells under the retina of the patient's left eye. The hope is that the cells will not be rejected by the patient's body and will regenerate the retina and restore her eyesight.

In a previous effort to use the controversial technique, a team of opthalmologists at the University of Rochester in New York reported "somewhat improved sight" among half the eight patients who received foetal eye tissue to treat a rare inherited eye disorder.

Opponents of abortion have vehemently objected to transplants using cells from aborted foetuses. Among their concerns are that successful transplants will encourage abortions for the purpose of harvesting foetal tissue.

While President Bill Clinton lifted a ban against foetal cell research in 1993, scientists have sometimes been reluctant to pursue such research because of ethical problems raised by the heated debate over abortion.

Scientists have experimented with transplanted foetal tissue in efforts to treat several adult neurological diseases such as Parkinson's and Alzheimer's, with some success. The technique might also prove fruitful in battling diabetes, leukaemia, and immune disorders.

"We've learned how to grow these cells quite successfully in culture and implant them in different animal models," said J. Terry Ernest, chairman of opthalmology at the university who performed the surgery with retinal surgeon Samir Patel.

Ernest defended the use of foetal tissue from second-trimester abortions, which he called "tragedies" because they were performed only because the foetus was hopelessly abnormal or because the pregnancy posed a threat to the mother's health.
Before the cells were harvested for this week's eye transplant, the mother of the aborted foetus signed a lengthy consent form that required testing for diseases including the AIDS virus.
